written.title: Is checkout B ready to launch?
written.mission: You are a junior web analyst at Brindle Cart. Recommend **whether checkout B should replace checkout A**, using evidence the product team can explain and act on.
written.deadline: Give {{product}} a recommendation today at 3 p.m.

panels.title: First look at the checkout experiment

metrics.label: Available traffic
metrics.note: Visitors can be split equally between A and B.

panels.note: Visitors were randomly assigned. B changes a shipping message; prices and checkout steps stay the same. No sample size or stopping rule was set.

team.expertise: Checks whether experiments can separate a real effect from chance.
Wants a useful checkout improvement without delaying other work.
Calculates test results and sample sizes for people to review.

skills.name: Tell a real difference from chance
skills.practice: Write two sentences explaining why 60 purchases versus 50 does not, by itself, establish that one checkout works better.

skills.name: Choose a sample size
skills.practice: Draft one AI request that includes the starting purchase rate, the improvement worth detecting, and a request for a sample-size explanation.

skills.name: Explain a test result
skills.practice: Explain one experiment result in two sentences: what the evidence supports and what it does not promise.

messages.text: B got 10 more purchases with the same number of visitors. The change is cheap to release. Can we call it a winner today?
Random groups can differ even when a change does nothing. Hypothesis testing checks how surprising our results would be if there were no real difference.

nodes.prompt: How do you prepare your recommendation?

choices.text: Use the current purchase rates to prepare a decision for today's meeting.

replies.text: That keeps us moving. I'll need you to explain how much confidence we should put in the gap.
We still haven't checked how much random variation could explain.

notes.text: You compared the rates, but the size of the gap alone cannot tell you whether chance is a reasonable explanation.
notes.example: Ask for a test of the current gap before describing B as a winner.

choices.text: Ask {{ai}} to check the gap and plan a test for the improvement we care about.

replies.text: The current gap is not strong evidence against chance. To detect a change from 5% to 6%, a common planning calculation gives about 8,200 visitors per version.
I'll review the calculation and the assumptions before we choose a plan.

notes.text: You tied the sample-size request to the starting rate and the improvement the business wants to detect.
You used AI to check the evidence rather than asking it to justify a launch.

messages.text: I checked the plan: about 8,200 per version gives roughly an 80% chance of detecting the target improvement. We'll use a rule that falsely flags a difference about 5% of the time when there is none.
Those are planning settings, not guarantees. Treat today's results as an early look and use fresh visitors for the planned test, without stopping early when B looks ahead.
At our traffic level, that's about 14 days. Waiting is manageable, but it pushes back the launch and ties up our experiment slot.

nodes.prompt: What plan do you agree to?

choices.text: Run the fresh test to 8,200 visitors per version, then make the launch decision.

replies.text: I'll reserve the experiment slot and move the launch review. We can make today's meeting about approving the plan.
We'll keep the assignment random and compare purchase rates once the planned sample is complete.

panel.title: Fresh test: planned sample complete
panel.note: Only fresh-test visitors are included. The team reached the planned sample without stopping early.

notes.text: You accepted a real scheduling cost to collect enough observations for the improvement that matters.
You set the stopping rule before collecting fresh data, rather than stopping whenever the result looked favorable.

choices.text: Keep the experiment slot free and make today's decision from the first 2,000 visits.

replies.text: That avoids the delay. We still need to decide whether this supports a launch or just a promising lead.
The sample-size calculation doesn't strengthen the data we already have. The initial gap is still uncertain.

notes.text: You identified the needed sample but chose not to collect it. Keep the recommendation tentative rather than treating the planning work as new evidence.
notes.example: "B looks promising, but we have not collected enough evidence to call it better."

messages.text: We're still looking at 50 purchases for A and 60 for B, out of 1,000 visits each. What should I put in today's decision note?
A launch decision and a claim that B truly works better are different things. We can choose a business action without pretending the evidence is stronger than it is.

nodes.prompt: What do you recommend with the evidence available?

choices.text: Launch B and report that its higher purchase rate shows the new message works.

replies.text: I'll launch it and schedule a review. But our launch note will be leaning heavily on just 10 extra purchases.
That gap could still be chance. Watching purchases after launch won't replace a planned comparison with A.

notes.text: You treated an observed lead as evidence of a real effect. A larger planned comparison is needed to make that claim responsibly.
Separate a decision to launch from a conclusion that the experiment established a benefit.
notes.example: "We are launching a promising change, but this early comparison has not established that it increases purchases."

choices.text: Keep A for now and request a planned test before calling B the better checkout.

replies.text: I'll review the sample target and stopping rule before new visitors enter the test. Today's results will remain an early look.
I'll mark the result as inconclusive and find room for the test. That delays the release, but gives us a defensible next step.

notes.text: You left room for chance instead of turning a promising result into a firm conclusion.
You paired uncertainty with a concrete next step, so the team can act without overstating what it knows.

messages.text: The fresh test gives a p-value of about 0.005. If A and B were equally effective, a gap at least this large in either direction would occur about 0.5% of the time under this test's assumptions.

written.title: What sales total can you trust?
written.mission: You’re a junior data analyst preparing yesterday’s sales report. Deliver **a checked sales total** and a short record of anything you changed.
written.deadline: Send the report to {{sales}} by 10:00 a.m.

panels.title: Yesterday’s sales export

metrics.label: Rows
metrics.note: Each row should represent one sold item.

metrics.label: Recorded amounts
metrics.note: Sum of the amounts that are filled in.

metrics.label: Missing amounts
metrics.note: A blank is not necessarily a $0 sale.

metrics.label: Payment labels
metrics.note: These labels all mean the payment was received.

panels.note: The original export is saved. Item-line IDs identify individual items; one order can contain several items.

team.expertise: Knows the export and can check item lines against the original sales records.
Needs a usable total for the morning planning meeting.
Can scan rows, suggest cleanup steps, and calculate totals for you to check.

skills.name: Find messy data
skills.practice: Inspect eight sample rows and mark one duplicate, one blank, and one inconsistent label.

skills.name: Clean safely and record changes
skills.practice: Write a three-line change log showing what you changed, why, and which source supported it.

skills.name: Check AI cleanup
skills.practice: Check one AI cleanup suggestion against the original rows, then independently recalculate its total.

messages.text: Can you get me yesterday’s total before the meeting? The export already adds up to $132.00.
Data cleaning means finding and fixing problems before using the data. Watch for duplicates—extra copies of the same item line—but remember that two items can belong to the same order.
I can inspect the export and propose changes without editing the original. You’ll still need to check my suggestions.

nodes.prompt: How do you start?

choices.text: Standardize the payment labels first; leave the row checks for the final pass.

replies.text: The labels now all read “Paid” in a working copy. The eight rows, the blank amount, and the $132.00 recorded sum are unchanged.
That’s a start. I still need a number I can use.

notes.text: You recognized that different capitalization can describe the same payment status.
Label cleanup does not resolve missing amounts or extra rows. Keep the total on hold until those checks are complete.
notes.example: "The labels are consistent, but the sales total is not checked yet."

choices.text: Ask {{ai}} to flag duplicates, blanks, and label differences without changing the export.

replies.text: I found a repeated order number and one blank amount. My proposed cleanup keeps the first row for each order, removes the blank row, and standardizes the payment labels. That leaves five rows totaling $87.00.
That’s a proposal, not a checked result. We need to inspect which rows would disappear.

notes.text: You used AI to surface possible problems while keeping its proposed edits separate from the original.

messages.text: The proposed removals are a second copy of item line L101 for $20.00, item line L103 for $25.00 because its order number repeats, and item line L104 because its amount is blank.
L102 and L103 are different items on the same order. I can check L101 and the missing amount against the original sales records.
A full check uses the time I wanted for reviewing the report. Can we finish with what we have?

nodes.prompt: What do you do with the AI’s proposed cleanup?

choices.text: Use the $87.00 result and note that AI removed repeated orders and blank amounts.

replies.text: I’ve put $87.00 into the meeting report.
That drops a real $25.00 item. The blank amount is also still unknown, so five rows is not a verified set of sales.

notes.text: The AI used order numbers to remove rows even though an order can contain several items. Check the meaning of an identifier before accepting duplicate removal.
notes.example: Compare item-line IDs and row contents, not order numbers alone.

notes.text: A blank amount is unresolved information, not evidence that a sale should be deleted.
notes.example: Look up L104 in the original sales record before deciding what to change.

choices.text: Check the flagged lines with {{data}}, then recalculate and record only supported changes.

replies.text: The source confirms L101 is an exact duplicate and L104 should be $18.00. Keep both L102 and L103: they are separate items.
With those corrections, seven item lines total $130.00. The payment labels can all be standardized to “Paid.”
Your independent check matches: $132.00 − $20.00 + $18.00 = $130.00. The working copy and change log are saved beside the untouched export.

panel.title: Checked sales report
panel.note: Original preserved; row changes and supporting sources recorded.

notes.text: You challenged the AI’s rule, checked the affected records, and independently reconciled the total.
You removed only a confirmed duplicate, filled a blank from a reliable source, and kept a change log.

choices.text: Withhold the total for this meeting and send the flagged rows for a later source check.

replies.text: I’ll leave yesterday’s total out and explain that it is still being checked.
The original eight rows are preserved. We haven’t resolved the duplicate or blank, so neither $132.00 nor $87.00 is ready to report.

notes.text: You kept an unverified AI result out of the report.
Holding the total is safe, but the source check was available before the deadline. A focused check could have delivered a usable number.
notes.example: Ask for confirmation of L101 and the source amount for L104.

messages.text: The labels are fixed, but the row checks are still open. The export includes two copies of L101 and two different item lines, L102 and L103, on one order.
Could we just keep one row per order and leave out the blank? I need to start preparing the meeting report.
I can compare the item lines and calculate a revised total once the source records confirm what should change.

nodes.prompt: How do you finish the report?

choices.text: Send the label-cleaned file as unfinished and withhold the sales total until a later check.

replies.text: I’ll leave the total out of this meeting.
The eight rows remain intact, with their labels standardized. The $132.00 recorded sum is still incomplete and may include an extra row.

notes.text: You clearly separated a partially cleaned file from a report-ready result.
Prioritize problems that affect the total before cosmetic differences such as capitalization.
notes.example: Check repeated item lines and missing amounts before formatting labels.

choices.text: Keep the first row for each order, drop the blank amount, and send the resulting total.

replies.text: That rule leaves five rows totaling $87.00. It removes a $20.00 copy of L101, the separate $25.00 item L103, and the blank L104.
I’ve used $87.00 in the meeting report.
L103 is a real item, not a duplicate. We also haven’t checked the missing amount, so this report needs correction.

notes.text: Repeated order numbers do not prove that rows are duplicates. Different items can share an order.
notes.example: Use the item-line ID and matching row details to investigate duplicates.

notes.text: Removing a blank row hides the missing information rather than resolving it.
notes.example: Check the original record or keep the amount explicitly unresolved.

choices.text: Check the suspect lines with {{data}}, then ask {{ai}} to total the supported corrections.

replies.text: The source confirms one exact extra copy of L101 for $20.00. L102 and L103 are separate items, and the blank L104 should be $18.00.
Removing only that extra copy and restoring $18.00 gives seven item lines totaling $130.00.
Your own check agrees: $132.00 − $20.00 + $18.00 = $130.00. We’ve saved the corrected copy and a change log without altering the original.

panel.title: Checked sales report
panel.note: Original preserved; row changes and supporting sources recorded.

notes.text: You distinguished an extra copy of an item from separate items on the same order.
You gave AI source-supported corrections and checked its arithmetic before using the result.

endings.outcome: {{sales}} receives a checked total of $130.00 across seven item lines before the meeting, with less time for review. The original export and change log make the corrections traceable.
The meeting goes ahead without yesterday’s sales total. You avoid presenting an unchecked number, but the duplicate and missing amount still need source checks.
The meeting report uses $87.00 across five rows, including the mistaken removal of a real $25.00 item. {{data}} flags the report for correction; the missing amount still needs checking.

summary: A repeated identifier is only a duplicate if it identifies something that should appear once.
Resolve missing values from a reliable source, preserve the original, and record supported changes.
Check an AI’s cleanup rules and affected rows before trusting its final total.

written.title: Dá para ouvir a luz chegando em pacotes?
written.mission: Explore uma máquina que transforma chegadas de luz em cliques. Seu desafio é **descobrir como a luz chega em pacotes e ainda forma desenhos de onda**.

panels.title: Sua bancada imaginária

metrics.label: Fonte de luz
metrics.note: Você pode mudar o brilho sem mudar a cor.

metrics.label: Detector
metrics.note: A máquina transforma cada detecção em som.

panels.note: A luz não faz esse som sozinha: os cliques são produzidos pelo aparelho.

team.expertise: Ajuda você a ligar as observações às ideias da física.
Ajusta a fonte e registra as chegadas de luz.

skills.name: Explicar os pacotes de energia
skills.practice: Explique em duas frases o que muda ao diminuir o brilho de uma luz sem mudar sua cor: a quantidade de pacotes ou a energia de cada pacote?

skills.name: Reconhecer onda e partícula
skills.practice: Faça dois desenhos pequenos: as chegadas isoladas de luz e o padrão de faixas formado por muitas chegadas. Escreva o que cada desenho revela.

messages.text: A máquina está pronta. Posso deixar a luz fraquinha ou aumentar o brilho, mantendo a mesma cor.
Um quantum é um pacote de energia. No caso da luz, esse pacote é chamado de fóton. Vamos procurar uma pista desses pacotes?

nodes.prompt: Como você quer começar a escutar a luz?

choices.text: Aumentar o brilho e gravar os cliques para ter bastante sinal logo.

replies.text: Temos muitos cliques próximos uns dos outros. A gravação ajuda, mas fica difícil distinguir cada chegada só pelo ouvido.
Mais brilho trouxe mais pacotes por segundo, não pacotes maiores. Para essa mesma cor, a energia de cada fóton continua igual.

notes.text: Um sinal forte é fácil de perceber, mas pode esconder as chegadas separadas. Reduzir o brilho, mantendo a cor, ajuda a investigar os pacotes.
notes.example: “Vamos diminuir o número de chegadas para ouvir cada uma separadamente.”

choices.text: Diminuir o brilho e pedir o registro dos cliques separados.

replies.text: Clique… silêncio… clique. Ao reduzir o brilho, as chegadas ficam mais espaçadas, em vez de virarem uma chegada contínua cada vez menor.
Para essa mesma cor, cada fóton carrega a mesma energia. Diminuir o brilho reduz quantos pacotes chegam por segundo.

notes.text: Você manteve a cor e mudou apenas o brilho. Isso ajuda a separar a energia de cada pacote da quantidade de pacotes que chegam.
notes.example: “A luz mais fraca traz menos pacotes por segundo, não uma fração de cada pacote.”

messages.text: Agora há duas fendas estreitas entre a fonte e uma tela que marca onde a luz chega. Vou usar luz bem fraca, com os fótons atravessando o aparelho um de cada vez.
Não vamos medir por qual fenda cada fóton passa. Cada chegada deixa um ponto na tela. Você prefere uma olhada rápida ou esperar o desenho crescer?

nodes.prompt: O laboratório fecha em breve. O que você faz com o tempo que resta?

choices.text: Ficar mais alguns minutos e juntar muitos pontos na mesma tela.

replies.text: Os pontos continuam chegando um a um. Aos poucos, aparecem faixas com muitos pontos, separadas por faixas com poucos.
Esse padrão de interferência é uma marca do comportamento de onda. As chegadas são localizadas, como partículas, mas o desenho de muitas chegadas revela o lado de onda da luz.

metrics.label: Muitas chegadas
metrics.note: Regiões com muitos pontos e regiões com poucos.

panel.note: O padrão aparece no conjunto, mesmo com chegadas individuais.

notes.text: Você observou tanto os eventos separados quanto o desenho coletivo. São pistas diferentes: uma mostra chegadas localizadas; a outra revela comportamento de onda.

choices.text: Guardar só os primeiros pontos e liberar a bancada mais cedo.

replies.text: Salvei a imagem. Há poucos pontos espalhados, sem um desenho claro. Liberamos a bancada, mas esse registro ainda não mostra como os pontos se distribuem.
Uma chegada localizada não conta a história toda. Com tão poucos pontos, não dá para concluir se o conjunto forma um padrão de onda.

notes.text: Encerrar cedo poupou tempo, mas deixou pouca evidência sobre o comportamento de onda. Antes de concluir, acompanhe o desenho formado por muitas chegadas.
notes.example: “Já vimos pontos separados; falta observar o padrão que muitos pontos formam.”

endings.outcome: Você sai com um registro de chegadas individuais que, juntas, formam faixas de interferência. A mesma luz oferece pistas de pacotes de energia e de comportamento de onda.
Você libera a bancada mais cedo e leva uma imagem com poucos pontos. O registro mostra chegadas localizadas, mas a investigação do comportamento de onda fica para outra visita.

summary: Para uma luz de uma única cor bem definida, diminuir o brilho reduz a quantidade de fótons que chegam por segundo, não a energia de cada fóton.
A luz apresenta dualidade onda-partícula: é detectada em chegadas localizadas e pode formar padrões de interferência característicos de ondas.

written.title: Dá para ouvir a luz chegando em pacotes?
written.mission: Explore uma máquina que transforma chegadas de luz em cliques. Seu desafio é **descobrir como a luz chega em pacotes e ainda forma desenhos de onda**.

panels.title: Sua bancada imaginária

metrics.label: Fonte de luz
metrics.note: Você pode mudar o brilho sem mudar a cor.

metrics.label: Detector
metrics.note: A máquina transforma cada detecção em som.

panels.note: A luz não faz esse som sozinha: os cliques são produzidos pelo aparelho.

team.expertise: Ajuda você a ligar as observações às ideias da física.

skills.name: Explicar os pacotes de energia
skills.practice: Explique em duas frases o que muda ao diminuir o brilho de uma luz sem mudar sua cor: a quantidade de pacotes ou a energia de cada pacote?

skills.name: Reconhecer onda e partícula
skills.practice: Faça dois desenhos pequenos: as chegadas isoladas de luz e o padrão de faixas formado por muitas chegadas. Escreva o que cada desenho revela.

messages.text: A máquina está pronta. Posso deixar a luz fraquinha ou aumentar o brilho, mantendo a mesma cor.
Um quantum é um pacote de energia. No caso da luz, esse pacote é chamado de fóton. Vamos procurar uma pista desses pacotes?

nodes.prompt: Como você quer começar a escutar a luz?

choices.text: Aumentar o brilho e gravar os cliques para ter bastante sinal logo.

replies.text: Temos muitos cliques próximos uns dos outros. A gravação ajuda, mas fica difícil distinguir cada chegada só pelo ouvido.
Mais brilho trouxe mais pacotes por segundo, não pacotes maiores. Para essa mesma cor, a energia de cada fóton continua igual.

notes.text: Um sinal forte é fácil de perceber, mas pode esconder as chegadas separadas. Reduzir o brilho, mantendo a cor, ajuda a investigar os pacotes.
notes.example: “Vamos diminuir o número de chegadas para ouvir cada uma separadamente.”

choices.text: Diminuir o brilho e pedir o registro dos cliques separados.

replies.text: Clique… silêncio… clique. Ao reduzir o brilho, as chegadas ficam mais espaçadas, em vez de virarem uma chegada contínua cada vez menor.
